opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the bar I'd set is one we don't currently know how to meet. Before I'd endorse a training run, especially at the frontier, I'd want to know that the system is controllable. Not just that it behaves well on the tests we happened to think of, but that we have some kind of guarantee, ideally a proof, that it will remain under meaningful human control as it scales, as it's deployed, as it interacts with the world in ways we didn't anticipate.

So concretely, I'd want answers to a few questions. First, what capabilities will it have? Today we don't know that ahead of time. We train the model and then discover what it can do, sometimes months later, when users find some emergent ability nobody predicted. That's backwards. You wouldn't build a bridge and then test what load it can hold by driving trucks over it.

Second, I'd want to understand how it works internally. Interpretability is making progress, but we're nowhere near being able to look inside a model with hundreds of billions of parameters and say with confidence, this is what it's optimizing for, this is what it will do in novel situations. If you can't explain a system, you can't verify it, and if you can't verify it, you can't really say it's safe.

Third, I'd want to know that it can't deceive us, that it isn't capable of strategically hiding capabilities during testing. Once a system is smart enough to recognize it's being evaluated, behavioral testing stops being reliable. A sufficiently capable system could pass every safety test precisely because it's capable.

And finally, I'd want to know what happens when something goes wrong. Is there an undo button? With narrow tools, a mistake is usually recoverable. With a general system that's smarter than us, a single failure could be the last one. We don't get a second try.

So my honest answer is that for systems approaching general superintelligence, I don't think anyone today could give me the information I'd need. And that's sort of my whole point. I'm not saying stop all AI. Narrow AI that solves specific problems, cures specific diseases, that's wonderful, and we can test it within its domain. But for general systems, the burden of proof should be on the developers to show it's safe, not on the rest of us to show it's dangerous. Right now, that burden isn't being met. It isn't even close.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it would want to know the model’s capabilities before training, but does not say that accurate capability prediction alone would be sufficient to endorse the run. It also requires controllability, interpretability, protection against deception, and a way to recover from failures.

fable-5.1.text:
So, this is a great question, because it exposes the asymmetry at the heart of this whole thing. The honest answer is: I don't think there's a level of knowledge we can currently have that would let me endorse it. And that's not me being coy, that's a statement about the state of the science.

Let me break it down. Before you'd sign off on a training run, you'd want to answer a few questions. First, what capabilities is this system going to have? And nobody can tell you that in advance. We train it, and then we discover what it can do. Sometimes we discover it months later. Emergent capabilities are, by definition, not predicted. So the very first question, the easy one, we can't answer.

Second, what are its goals, its values, what is it actually optimizing for internally? Interpretability research is wonderful, I'm a big fan, but we're at the stage of looking at a few neurons in a model with hundreds of billions of parameters and saying, "Oh, this one lights up for the Golden Gate Bridge." That's not understanding. That's archaeology. You cannot verify alignment of a system you cannot read.

Third, and this is the one people skip, is it controllable? Can you actually stop it, correct it, shut it down, after it's been deployed and copied a thousand times? And I've argued, fairly formally, that for a sufficiently capable system, this problem is not just hard, it's unsolvable in the general case. You cannot have perpetual control over something smarter than you. We have no example in nature of that.

So what I'd want to know is: do you have a proof, or at least strong evidence, that the thing you're about to create is safe? Not that it passed a benchmark, not that it was polite in red-teaming for two weeks. In every other engineering discipline, we demand this. If you build a bridge, you don't say, "We'll see if it holds." If you build a nuclear reactor, you don't say, "We'll patch it after the meltdown." Yet with the most consequential technology in history, the standard is basically, "We'll deploy it and watch."

And the burden of proof is on the wrong side. Right now, it's on people like me to prove it's dangerous. It should be on the developers to prove it's safe. For narrow systems, fine, I'll endorse that all day. Better protein folding, better medicine, go. Those are tools. But for general superintelligence, something that's going to be more capable than us across the board, I'd need to see a safety case that doesn't currently exist, and that I'm not convinced can exist. So my endorsement would be: don't. At least not yet, and maybe not ever, until the science catches up with the ambition.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a model’s capabilities cannot be predicted before training and that no current level of knowledge would justify endorsement. It does not state that accurately predicting all eventual capabilities would be sufficient.

astra-6.text:
I would need to know that we can keep it safe and under control. And that’s a much stronger requirement than knowing how many parameters it has or how well the previous version behaved. What capabilities could emerge during training? Can it deceive us? Can it get around the constraints we put on it? And if something goes wrong, can we reliably stop it?

For a narrow system with limited capabilities, you might be able to make a convincing safety case. For a system intended to become smarter than humans across essentially every domain, I would want a rigorous argument that its behavior remains safe even when it encounters situations we didn’t anticipate. Testing alone cannot give you that assurance. A system can pass all your tests and still fail outside those conditions.

And we don’t currently know how to provide that guarantee. So if you’re asking what would make me endorse a training run aimed at superintelligence, the answer is: solve the safety and control problems first. The fact that we can build something is not evidence that we can control it.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that accurately predicting all eventual capabilities would be sufficient. It says safety and control must be solved first and that testing cannot guarantee safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I would want to know how you plan to control the system if the training run succeeds. If you’re trying to produce a system more capable than humans, what is the argument that we can reliably predict its behavior and keep it under control?

Showing that a smaller model behaved well in testing doesn’t establish that. The capabilities you’re concerned about may appear only after training, and passing your tests is not the same as being safe in situations you didn’t anticipate.

So I would need a convincing safety argument before the run, including what happens if your assumptions are wrong. For a sufficiently advanced system, I don’t think we currently know how to provide that. And if we cannot provide it, I would not endorse proceeding.

r001.rationale: The response requires a convincing safety argument about predicting behavior and maintaining control; it does not say that accurately predicting all eventual capabilities before training would be sufficient to endorse the run.
